cards.headline: An English company lands in Powhatan's country.
cards.lede: In May 1607, 104 English men and boys built a fort on the James River, inside the land of about 30 tribes that paid tribute to one leader, Powhatan.
body: The English call the place Virginia. The people who live there call it Tsenacomoco: about 15,000 people, by modern estimates, in towns of bark- and mat-covered houses, with fields of corn, beans and squash. They outnumber the English by more than a hundred to one.

There is no African in the colony. The first documented Africans arrive in 1619, twelve years from now (the first line of your Document 13). There is no English woman either: the first two come in 1608.

The King's charter promises the colonists every liberty of the English (the King's card). It promises nothing to the people already here. Within ten years an epidemic will empty Native towns on the New England coast (your Document 2).
So the line starts here, with three arcs not yet begun and a fourth people, the Powhatan, who are not waiting for anyone's promise.

cards.headline: Being 16 in 1607
cards.lede: What it was like to be sixteen in 1607, set beside what it's like to be a teenager now.

rows.heading: AT 16, I'D BE…
rows.then: If I am English, in Virginia: one of the boys who came with the first men, cutting timber and hauling water for the fort. Thomas Savage, about 13, and Henry Spelman, about 14, were later sent to live with the Powhatan to learn their language, and became interpreters. If I am Powhatan: a boy learns to fish and hunt; a girl works the gardens of corn, beans and squash with the women. There is no school in the colony.
rows.now: In school: New York law requires it until at least 16. Working papers from 14.

rows.heading: WHO DECIDED FOR ME
rows.then: If I am English: my father or my master, and in the fort the council the Virginia Company named. If I am Powhatan: my family, my town's leader, and above him Powhatan.
rows.now: Parents or guardians until 18, the age of majority in New York; the school for the school day.

rows.heading: HOW I'D GET THE NEWS
rows.then: By word of mouth, and by letters carried by ship, months late. There is no newspaper anywhere in English America. London learns about Jamestown from John Smith's A True Relation, printed in 1608.
rows.now: A phone. In 2023 about 95 of every 100 U.S. teens said they had access to a smartphone.

rows.heading: HOW FAR I'D GO
rows.then: The crossing from England took about four months, December 1606 to April 1607. In Virginia, as far as a canoe or my own feet go.
rows.now: A learner permit at 16 in New York; a bus, a car, a plane. Farther in an afternoon than the 1850 kid went in a year.

rows.heading: WHAT WAS MINE TO DECIDE
rows.then: Almost nothing. Between 1617 and 1623, London's parishes shipped about 250 poor children to Virginia, and many of them did not want to go.
rows.now: The vote at 18 (Twenty-sixth Amendment, 1971). Your own wages are yours.

cards.headline: A line down the mountains.
cards.lede: The King's new proclamation keeps the land west of the Appalachians for the Native nations, and forbids his colonists to settle on it or buy it.
body: The war is over, and Britain claims everything east of the Mississippi. The nations who live there did not sign the treaty. This spring many of them went to war against the British forts around the Great Lakes, and in October the King's government answered with a line.

About one person in five in the thirteen colonies is of African descent, nearly all of them enslaved for life by laws the colonies built one statute at a time (your Document 13). Venture Smith, kidnapped as a child, is enslaved in New England (Document 12).
A married woman's legal existence is suspended under her husband's (coverture); in two years an English judge will describe it in a book (Document 18).
So the line stands three ways at once. One America is not even a question yet: there are thirteen colonies, a King, and the nations the King's line is drawn around.

cards.headline: Nine years after "Join, or Die."
cards.lede: The colonies never did join. The war against France was won with the King's army and navy and London's money, and now London decides what comes next.
body: In 1754 Benjamin Franklin printed a snake cut into pieces, one for most of the colonies, with the words JOIN, OR DIE (your Document 16). That summer, delegates at Albany approved his plan for a union of the colonies.
No colonial assembly would adopt it. Each colony kept its own assembly, its own governor and its own taxes, and colonial soldiers fought beside the King's regulars, each colony on its own terms.

Now the war is over and the questions are London's to answer: where the colonists may live, how many soldiers stay, and who pays. A government can be too weak to protect its people. Can it also reach too far?

cards.headline: Being 16 in 1763
cards.lede: What it was like to be sixteen in 1763, set beside what it's like to be a teenager now.

rows.heading: AT 16, I'D BE…
rows.then: On a farm, almost surely. A boy in a trade is an apprentice, bound by a signed paper until 21: Benjamin Franklin was bound to his brother, a printer, at 12, and ran away at 17. A New England girl learns to read at home or at a dame school and learns the work of a household. One young person in five is of African descent, and nearly all of them are enslaved.
rows.now: In school: New York law requires it until at least 16. Working papers from 14.

rows.heading: WHO DECIDED FOR ME
rows.then: My father, by law, until I turn 21. If I am bound out, my master. If I am a girl who marries, my husband: a married woman's property and wages are his (coverture). If I am enslaved, the person who claims to own me.
rows.now: Parents or guardians until 18, the age of majority in New York; the school for the school day.

rows.heading: WHAT I'D WEAR
rows.then: A young woman: a gown open in front over a petticoat, a laced bodice, an apron, a linen cap, a shawl or cloak. A young man: a long coat, a waistcoat, knee breeches with stockings, buckled shoes, a three-cornered hat. rows.heading: HOW I'D GET THE NEWS
rows.then: A weekly newspaper, if my town has a printer, read aloud at the tavern or the meetinghouse. News from London comes by ship, a month or two behind. Franklin's paper ran the snake (Document 16).
rows.now: A phone. In 2023 about 95 of every 100 U.S. teens said they had access to a smartphone.

rows.heading: HOW FAR I'D GO
rows.then: As far as a horse walks in a day, or a sailing ship goes with the wind. Crossing the ocean to London takes one to two months.
rows.now: A learner permit at 16 in New York; a bus, a car, a plane. Farther in an afternoon than the 1850 kid went in a year.

rows.heading: WHAT WAS MINE TO DECIDE
rows.then: Almost nothing in law. The vote comes at 21, and only to men who own property. Most colonies enroll free white men in the militia from 16. A girl's property passes to her husband the day she marries.
rows.now: The vote at 18 (Twenty-sixth Amendment, 1971). Your own wages are yours.

cards.headline: Five million counted. One in six is enslaved.
cards.lede: The new census says 5,308,483 people live in the United States, and 893,602 of them are enslaved.
body: The promise of 1776 says all men are created equal. In 1801 the law counts three of every five enslaved people toward a state's seats in the House, and no enslaved person can vote, own property or keep a family together by right.
A married woman's legal existence is suspended under her husband's (coverture). Native nations are not counted at all: the Constitution says "Indians not taxed" are left out.
So the line stands where 1787 put it. The promise is written down. Who it reaches is still being decided.

cards.lede: Jefferson's party won by promising a smaller national government. Now it has to run one.
body: The Articles of Confederation (1781) were too weak to tax or keep order, so the Constitution (1787) built a stronger government and the Bill of Rights (1791) wrote down its limits. Federalists and Republicans have argued ever since about how much that government should do.

In his inaugural, Jefferson says the government should "restrain men from injuring one another" and otherwise leave them free. In his last weeks, President Adams filled new judgeships created by the Judiciary Act of 1801; the Republicans call them the midnight judges.

cards.headline: Being 16 in 1801
cards.lede: What it was like to be sixteen in 1801, set beside what it's like to be a teenager now.

rows.heading: AT 16, I'D BE…
rows.then: On a farm, almost surely: 94 of every 100 Americans live outside any town of 2,500 people. A boy in a trade is an apprentice, bound by a signed paper to his master until 21. A few winters of district school is the usual schooling; there is no public high school anywhere in the country yet. One young person in six is enslaved: working with no pay, and able to be sold.
rows.now: In school: New York law requires it until at least 16. Working papers from 14.

rows.heading: WHO DECIDED FOR ME
rows.then: My father, by law, until I turn 21. If I am bound out, my master. If I am a girl who marries, my husband: a married woman's property and wages are his (coverture). If I am enslaved, the person who claims to own me.
rows.now: Parents or guardians until 18, the age of majority in New York; the school for the school day.

rows.heading: WHAT I'D WEAR
rows.then: A young woman: a high-waisted gown, short sleeves, a cap or small bonnet, a shawl. A young man: a tailcoat, a cravat, knee breeches with stockings, a tall round hat. (Attire note: Leo's, from the silhouette prompts; not yet checked against a costume collection. Danny's gate.)
rows.now: Mostly your own choice, inside a dress code. Nothing here is about your closet.

rows.heading: HOW I'D GET THE NEWS
rows.then: A weekly newspaper, often read aloud at the tavern or the post office, days or weeks after the event. Since the Post Office Act of 1792, papers travel by mail cheaply, so a town paper reprints the city papers.
rows.now: A phone. In 2023 about 95 of every 100 U.S. teens said they had access to a smartphone.

rows.heading: HOW FAR I'D GO
rows.then: As far as a horse walks in a day, or a sailing ship goes with the wind. No canals of any length, no railroads, no steamboats (Fulton's first runs the Hudson in 1807).
rows.now: A learner permit at 16 in New York; a bus, a car, a plane. Farther in an afternoon than the 1850 kid went in a year.

rows.heading: WHAT WAS MINE TO DECIDE
rows.then: Almost nothing in law. The vote comes at 21, and in most states only to white men who own property. At 18 every free white man is enrolled in the militia whether he chooses it or not (Militia Act of 1792). A girl's property passes to her husband the day she marries.
rows.now: The vote at 18 (Twenty-sixth Amendment, 1971). Your own wages are yours.

Free Black young people: counted, and in most states barred from voting at 21 anyway. Girls: everything above says "he" for a reason.

This March his Court ruled that Congress's power over trade between the states covers steamboats (Gibbons v. Ogden, the Outside Information box in Casefile C).
The president reads the Constitution more narrowly than his Chief Justice. How much should the national government build, and who decides what it may do?

This year Jackson won the most electoral votes for president. Nothing on this line moves in 1824; the next time the country goes to war, this is the thread to open first.

rows.now: In school: New York law requires it until at least 16. Working papers from 14.

rows.heading: WHO DECIDED FOR ME
rows.then: My father, by law, until I turn 21. If I am bound out, my master. If I am a girl who marries, my husband: her property and wages are his (coverture). If I am enslaved, the person who claims to own me.
rows.now: Parents or guardians until 18, the age of majority in New York; the school for the school day.

rows.heading: WHAT I'D WEAR
rows.then: A young woman: a high-waisted gown, the waist starting to drop and the sleeves to fill out, a bonnet, a shawl. A young man: a tailcoat, a high collar and a cravat, and long trousers, which have replaced knee breeches for most young men. In New York the 1821 constitution let a white man vote if he paid a tax or served in the militia; a Black man needed $250 of property. A woman: no vote. At 18, the militia (the Militia Act of 1792 is still the law).

cards.headline: California free. A fugitive law with no jury.
cards.lede: On Sept. 9 California entered the Union as a free state. On Sept. 18 the president signed a law letting a federal commissioner send an accused fugitive south with no jury and no chance to testify.
body: Twenty-three million people are counted this year; 3,204,313 of them are enslaved, on separate schedules that list them by age and sex, not by name.

Two years ago at Seneca Falls, women declared that a married woman is "civilly dead" in the eye of the law (your Document 11). Twelve years ago the army marched the Cherokee west on the Trail of Tears (Documents 5 and 6). The people of the Mexican Cession became Americans in 1848 whether they chose it or not.
The promise is still written down. Every arc of this thread is being argued out loud now.

oi.fact: Under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 a commissioner was paid $10 if he ruled the accused a slave and $5 if he ruled the person free.

cards.headline: A canal across Central America: nobody builds it alone.
cards.lede: In April the United States and Britain agreed that neither would control a canal across Central America by itself (the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty).
body: The Monroe Doctrine (1823) told Europe to stay out of the Western Hemisphere. Then the United States fought a war with Mexico (1846–1848) and took a third of Mexico's land (Document 10 calls the war unjust).

In December, Fillmore will tell Congress it is "an imperative duty not to interfere in the government or internal policy of other nations." The country intervenes next door and says it does not intervene.

cards.headline: A president dies. His successor signs what he would not.
cards.lede: Zachary Taylor died on July 9. Millard Fillmore took the oath the next day, and in September signed all five compromise laws.
body: Jackson vetoed the bank and let Georgia ignore the Supreme Court (Documents 4 and 7). Polk sent troops into disputed land and got his war (Document 10). The presidency has grown by what presidents did when the Constitution was silent.
Now the office changes hands by a death, for the second time in the country's history. No election chose the man who signed the fugitive law.

cards.headline: Being 16 in 1850
cards.lede: What it was like to be sixteen in 1850, set beside what it's like to be a teenager now.

rows.heading: AT 16, I'D BE…
rows.then: Most likely still on a farm: 85 of every 100 Americans live outside any town. But a mill is possible now. In Lowell, Massachusetts, girls started in the mills at 10 or 11 (Lucy Larcom started at 11, in 1835), twelve hours a day, six days a week. This year's census asks, for the first time, whether you attended school in the past year. A public high school is still rare. One young person in seven is enslaved, and this year's law reaches into the free states to take back anyone who ran.
rows.now: In school: New York law requires it until at least 16. Working papers from 14.

rows.heading: WHO DECIDED FOR ME
rows.then: My father, by law, until 21. In a mill, the overseer and the bell. A married woman is "civilly dead" in the eye of the law: the words are Seneca Falls', 1848 (Document 11). If I am enslaved, the person who claims to own me, and now any federal commissioner.
rows.now: Parents or guardians until 18, the age of majority in New York; the school for the school day.

rows.heading: WHAT I'D WEAR
rows.then: A young woman: a fitted bodice, a wide bell skirt over petticoats, long sleeves, a bonnet tied under the chin, a shawl. A young man: a frock coat over a waistcoat, straight trousers, a cravat, a tall stovepipe hat. (Attire note: Leo's, from the silhouette prompts; not yet checked against a costume collection. Danny's gate.)
rows.now: Mostly your own choice, inside a dress code. Nothing here is about your closet.

rows.heading: HOW I'D GET THE NEWS
rows.then: A daily paper for a penny in a city (the New York Sun since 1833). News moves by telegraph since 1844, so a city paper can print yesterday's news from Washington. In the country, still days behind.
rows.now: A phone. In 2023 about 95 of every 100 U.S. teens said they had access to a smartphone.

rows.heading: HOW FAR I'D GO
rows.then: By canal boat, steamboat or train. The Erie Canal has run across New York since 1825, and the country has about 9,000 miles of railroad this year, up from 23 miles in 1830. Last year tens of thousands went to California by wagon or by ship.
rows.now: A learner permit at 16 in New York; a bus, a car, a plane. Farther in an afternoon than the 1850 kid went in a year.

rows.heading: WHAT WAS MINE TO DECIDE
rows.then: At 21, if I am a white man, the vote, in almost every state without owning property now. If I am a Black man in New York, only with $250 of property (the 1821 state constitution). If I am a woman, no vote, and my wages go to my husband. I can go west; I can sign on to a ship; I can sign a mill contract.
rows.now: The vote at 18 (Twenty-sixth Amendment, 1971). Your own wages are yours.

rows.text: Before 1825, nothing moved faster than a horse or the wind. The Erie Canal opened in 1825 (Document 3); then came the railroad. After: about 9,000 miles of track by 1850, and news by telegraph since 1844. A kid in 1850 can get farther in a day than a kid in 1801 could in a week.

The country kept buying and taking land: Louisiana (1803), Texas (1845), the Mexican Cession (1848). Every new piece raised the same question, whether slavery goes with it. The effect in 1850 is a Congress that has to pass five laws at once to keep the Union together, and a fugitive law that reaches into the free states.

Similar: in both years no woman votes, enslaved people are counted but not named, and Native nations are not counted at all. Different: the country grew from 5.3 million people to 23.2 million, and the enslaved population from 893,602 to 3,204,313. Watch the trap: the share of people enslaved fell (1 in 6 to 1 in 7) while the number more than tripled.
